prompt.context: Our client, a private equity firm, is considering acquiring a company that manufactures traditional toys. Toy Co., the potential acquisition, was founded in 1923 and is one of the world's largest traditional toy makers. The traditional toy industry is dominated by several large players and ToyCo is one of the top three players by sales volume in the space.
prompt.question: We have been hired to evaluate ToyCo's current strategy and to determine whether the private equity firm should place a bid to acquire the company. What considerations should the PE firm make in determining whether or not to acquire Toy Co.?

clarifying_info.q: What is the selling price of Toy Co.?
clarifying_info.a: The selling price of Toy Co. is irrelevant to the case discussion.

clarifying_info.q: Are there other firms interested in acquiring Toy Co.?
clarifying_info.a: We have no information about other firms interested in acquiring; assume there are none.

exhibits.title: Traditional Toy Sales, 2005-2016
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar or line chart showing annual traditional toy sales broken down by variety (Dolls, Action Figures, Outdoor Games, Blocks and Puzzles) from 2005 to 2016, with a note of 2% industry CAGR.
exhibits.data: Y-axis: dollar sales up to ~$7,000,000,000; categories: Dolls, Action Figures, Outdoor Games, Blocks and Puzzles; years 2005-2016; 2% industry CAGR labeled

framework: 1. Economics of Toy Co. — Revenue Streams (price/toy, number of customers) and Costs (materials, labor, distribution)
2. Market — Competition (new entrants, long-time rivals) and Customer preferences (rise of electronics, shifting toy variety preferences)
3. Exit Opportunities — Potential buyers and exit multiples for the PE firm

questions.prompt: Size the market for toys in the U.S. — estimate annual sales volume of toys in the U.S.
questions.guidance: Segment the population into buyer groups (parents, grandparents, older children, adult enthusiasts), estimate purchase frequency and average cart size per group, then multiply and sum. Strong candidates will proactively segment; interviewer may provide population figures if candidate estimates directionally correctly.

math.setup: Segment population into four buyer groups; for each group multiply: Population × Purchases per Year × Cart Size = Segment Market Size; sum all segments.
math.answer: ~$14.4 billion annual U.S. toy market (note: figures assume ~100 million U.S. households as the base)

questions.prompt: Show Exhibit 1: How has the market share of each toy variety changed over the past decade? What societal trends could have caused these shifts?
questions.guidance: Candidate should read the chart directionally and call out winners (Action Figures up from 26% to 40%, Outdoor Games up from 23% to 28%) and losers (Dolls down from 36% to 21%, Blocks and Puzzles down from 15% to 11%). Strong candidates link each shift to a societal trend without prompting.

math.setup: Read share percentages from exhibit data table for 2005 vs. 2016 per category.
steps: Action Figures: 26% (2005) → 40% (2016), increase of 14 percentage points
Outdoor Games: 23% (2005) → 28% (2016), increase of 5 percentage points
Blocks and Puzzles: 15% (2005) → 11% (2016), decline of 4 percentage points
math.answer: Action Figures gained the most share (+14pp); Dolls lost the most share (-15pp).

questions.prompt: Based on the Exhibit 1 analysis, what recommendations would you make to Toy Co. to better position its offerings to match consumer trends?
questions.guidance: Tests structured brainstorming organized by toy category. Strong candidates address each growing and declining segment with specific, actionable ideas and organize thoughts clearly by category.

brainstorming.prompt: Based on the market share trends in Exhibit 1, what recommendations would you make to Toy Co. to better position its offerings to match consumer trends?

categories.name: Action Figures
ideas: Aggressively pursue the action figures segment given its strong growth trend
Partner with movie studios or TV shows to build a more robust arsenal of characters
Focus on female character action figures to capture the declining popularity of dolls among girls

categories.name: Dolls
ideas: Focus on modern dolls that portray powerful female characters
Consider product lines similar to Barbie's introduction of dolls of different races, heights, and body types
Adjust production away from traditional dolls given greatest decline due to electronics and video games
Consider launching electronic versions of classic doll play to enter the non-traditional toy space

categories.name: Outdoor Games
ideas: Expand product offerings in outdoor games to capture push toward healthy living
Market outdoor toys as a screen-free, active alternative for parents

categories.name: Blocks and Puzzles
ideas: Explore electronic or digital hybrid versions of classic indoor games to combat cannibalization from electronics and video games

recommendation: The PE firm could go either way — acquire or not acquire — provided the reasoning is grounded in the PE context (buy, turn around, exit at a profit).
YES: There is movement in a growing industry segment (action figures, outdoor games) and under strong management Toy Co. can earn an even stronger market position.
NO: The industry's 2% CAGR is not compelling for PE returns and electronics will continue to encroach on the traditional toy space.
risks: As a legacy company (founded 1923), Toy Co. may resist new ownership and fail to implement recommendations
Electronics will continue to grow and take market share from traditional toys
Movie studios may begin manufacturing their own toys, causing Toy Co. to lose significant business in the action figure space
next_steps: Conduct deeper financial due diligence on Toy Co. — this case only examined the traditional toy market; understand unit economics and profitability before placing a bid
Begin planning how Toy Co.'s production can be rebalanced to respond to shifting market trends (scaling up action figures and outdoor toys, scaling down dolls)
